slides.body: Five mistakes to watch for.

items: Concluding "not backported" from git branch --contains <original>. Root cause: ancestry follows parent links, and a copy has no parent link to its original.
Concluding "not backported" from a plus sign in git cherry. Root cause: patch IDs pair textually identical diffs; an adapted copy, or one whose context differs, has another patch ID.
Backporting without -x. Root cause: the message line is the only record of the relationship that survives adaptation and travels with the history.
Treating "applied cleanly" as "works on the release". Root cause: the merge compared text in the files the commit touches; whether the release has what the fix depends on was never checked.
Generating a changelog from git log across lines that exchanged picks. Root cause: each picked change is two commits; anything that counts commits counts it twice unless --cherry-pick is used.

beats.text: Duplicates. In one sentence: after a cherry-pick the same change exists under two commit IDs, and git cherry and git log --cherry-mark find such pairs by comparing patch IDs.
beats.tele: Duplicates. In one sentence: after a cherry-pick the same change exists under two commit IDs, and `git cherry` and `git log --cherry-mark` find such pairs by comparing patch IDs.

beats.text: Precisely: git cherry <upstream> <head> lists the commits of <head> that are not in <upstream> and marks each with a minus if <upstream> contains a commit with the same patch ID, otherwise with a plus. git log --left-right --cherry-mark A...B walks both sides of the symmetric difference, the commits each side has and the other lacks, and marks such pairs with an equals sign. --cherry-pick in place of --cherry-mark leaves the pairs out.
beats.tele: Precisely: `git cherry <upstream> <head>` lists the commits of `<head>` that are not in `<upstream>` and marks each with a minus if `<upstream>` contains a commit with the same patch ID, otherwise with a plus. `git log --left-right --cherry-mark A...B` walks both sides of the symmetric difference, the commits each side has and the other lacks, and marks such pairs with an equals sign. `--cherry-pick` in place of `--cherry-mark` leaves the pairs out.

beats.text: Revert as the inverse. In one sentence: git revert <commit> 🟡 CAUTION is the same three-way merge with base and "theirs" exchanged: the base is the commit itself and "theirs" is its parent, so the change is applied backwards.
beats.tele: Revert as the inverse. In one sentence: `git revert <commit>` 🟡 CAUTION is the same three-way merge with base and "theirs" exchanged: the base is the commit itself and "theirs" is its parent, so the change is applied backwards.

beats.text: Read the two rows against each other: base and theirs change places, and ours stays HEAD.
beats.tele: Read the two rows against each other: base and theirs change places, and ours stays HEAD.

beats.text: Three witnesses, and each can testify only to what it saw.
beats.tele: Three witnesses, and each can testify only to what it saw.

beats.text: Ancestry saw parent links. It can say "this commit is reachable from that branch". It never saw a copy being made.
beats.tele: Ancestry saw parent links. It can say "this commit is reachable from that branch". It never saw a copy being made.

beats.text: The patch ID saw the text of a diff. It can say "these two commits make textually the same change". It can't recognise the same fix after it was adapted, or even after the surrounding lines differed.
beats.tele: The patch ID saw the text of a diff. It can say "these two commits make textually the same change". It can't recognise the same fix after it was adapted, or even after the surrounding lines differed.

beats.text: The message line written by -x is the only witness that was told, at the moment of the pick, "this is a copy of that". It can be wrong only if a person removed it or wrote it falsely.
beats.tele: The message line written by `-x` is the only witness that was told, at the moment of the pick, "this is a copy of that". It can be wrong only if a person removed it or wrote it falsely.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Concluding "not backported" from git branch --contains <original>. Root cause: ancestry follows parent links, and a copy has no parent link to its original.
beats.tele: Concluding "not backported" from `git branch --contains <original>`. Root cause: ancestry follows parent links, and a copy has no parent link to its original.

beats.text: Concluding "not backported" from a plus sign in git cherry. Root cause: patch IDs pair textually identical diffs; an adapted copy, or one whose context differs, has another patch ID.
beats.tele: Concluding "not backported" from a plus sign in `git cherry`. Root cause: patch IDs pair textually identical diffs; an adapted copy, or one whose context differs, has another patch ID.

beats.text: Backporting without -x. Root cause: the message line is the only record of the relationship that survives adaptation and travels with the history.
beats.tele: Backporting without `-x`. Root cause: the message line is the only record of the relationship that survives adaptation and travels with the history.

beats.text: Treating "applied cleanly" as "works on the release". Root cause: the merge compared text in the files the commit touches; whether the release has what the fix depends on was never checked.
beats.tele: Treating "applied cleanly" as "works on the release". Root cause: the merge compared text in the files the commit touches; whether the release has what the fix depends on was never checked.

beats.text: Generating a changelog from git log across lines that exchanged picks. Root cause: each picked change is two commits; anything that counts commits counts it twice unless --cherry-pick is used.

beats.text: The textbook's advice: record it where the sign-off lives. The -x line gives the auditor the original commit, and the original commit leads to the review and the tests. That is a chain from "what is running at the customer" to "who reviewed this change and what was tested", and it exists only because one option was typed.

That is a chain from "what is running at the customer" to "who reviewed this change and what was tested", and it exists only because one option was typed.

beats.text: The second point is for tooling. Anything that counts commits double-counts duplicates: a changelog generated from git log, a "commits since last release" metric. Generate such lists with --cherry-pick, and remember its limit: an adapted backport is invisible to patch comparison. Lab 10.3 works through that case.

beats.text: So a release team's standing answer to "is the fix in the release" has an order. First the -x line. Then patch comparison, read with its limit in mind. And when both are silent, the content of the file and a test. That first item is the evidence from the opening: the -x line would have settled the question at once.

beats.text: Patch IDs pair exact copies only, which is what git cherry and --cherry-mark report, and --cherry-pick removes such pairs from a comparison.
